Estimate Scales of Effect with Bayesian Inference

Source: R/bayes_scale_methods.R, R/multiScale_bayes.R
multiScale_bayes.Rd

Estimate landscape scales of effect and response coefficients together, as one posterior distribution that combines what the data say with the priors you state. Give each landscape predictor one shared scale, let the scale change with measured covariates, or let it vary among groups such as regions or years. This interface is experimental. A printed fit reports "Experimental Bayesian landscape-scale model".

Usage

# S3 method for class 'multiScaleR_bayes'
summary(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'multiScaleR_bayes'
print(x, ...)

multiScale_bayes(
  formula,
  inputs,
  data,
  scales = NULL,
  family = c("nbinom2", "poisson", "binomial", "gaussian"),
  row_id = NULL,
  priors = list(),
  method = c("sample", "prepare", "laplace", "marginal", "slice"),
  chains = 4L,
  iter = 2000L,
  warmup = floor(iter/2),
  seed = NULL,
  control = list(),
  laplace_draws = 2000L,
  cores = 1L
)

Arguments

object

A multiScaleR_bayes object from multiScale_bayes(), prepared or fitted.

...

Not used. Supplying any further argument is an error.

x

A multiScaleR_bayes object to print, prepared or fitted.

formula

Two-sided response formula, such as count ~ habitat + factor(year) + (1 | site). Name each landscape predictor as it is named in inputs. Its kernel-weighted value is computed at every candidate scale, so you never supply that column. The formula accepts fixed covariates, interactions with landscape predictors, offsets, and additive random intercepts. See "Write the response formula".

inputs

Prepared landscape inputs from kernel_prep() or kernel_prep_by_group(), built with a Gaussian or exponential kernel. Kernel means need the binned summaries (bin = TRUE, the default). Optimized weighted surface SQ needs the retained raw cell buffers and source specifications. Means and SQ can be combined. Distances, priors, and reported scales all use the projected map units of these inputs. Declared fixed-radius surface and landscape metrics enter as ordinary numeric covariates with their original preparation normalization, so keep their prepared columns in data. No scale is estimated for them, and a constant or undefined metric is an error.

data

Data frame with one row per observation, holding the response, fixed covariates, and grouping variables. Landscape predictors whose scales are estimated are rebuilt from inputs and need not appear here. A missing response or covariate value is an error. Rows are never dropped.

scales

Named list with one one-sided formula for each landscape predictor in formula, such as list(habitat = ~1 + (1 | year)). Each formula models the natural log of that predictor's scale. The default NULL gives every predictor one shared scale, the same as ~1. See "Write the scale formulas".

family

Response family, one of "nbinom2" (default, negative binomial with a log link), "poisson" (log link), "binomial" (logit link), or "gaussian" (identity link). See "Choose a response family".

row_id

Optional name of a column in data that matches each row to its prepared landscape, an entry of inputs$binned$point_ids (or a row name of inputs$kernel_dat for surface-only inputs). The default NULL matches the row names of data. IDs may repeat, so repeated visits can share one static landscape. With one map per year, use site-year IDs so each row reads the map for its own year. The name is kept with the fit and reused by predict() and simulate().

priors

Named list of prior settings to change. Settings you leave out take their defaults, and the default list() uses them all. See "Set the priors" for every setting and its default.

method

Computation, one of "sample" (default, NUTS sampling), "prepare", "slice", "laplace", or "marginal". The method changes how the posterior is computed, not the model, likelihood, or priors. "prepare" checks the data, formulas, priors, and bins without fitting. See "Choose a computation method".

chains

Number of independent chains for "sample" and "slice"; default 4. Chain diagnostics need at least two.

iter

Iterations per chain, including warmup; default 2000. Raise it when effective sample sizes fall short.

warmup

Iterations at the start of each chain that are discarded while the sampler tunes itself; default floor(iter / 2).

seed

Optional positive integer seed for sampling or approximation draws; default NULL. Slice, Laplace, and marginal fits restore your own random-number state after using a supplied seed. Slice sampling draws its chain seeds before any work is sent to workers, so a seed gives the same chains at every cores setting.

control

Named list of method-specific settings; default list() uses each method's defaults. NUTS accepts adapt_delta and max_treedepth. Slice sampling accepts no settings, so leave the list empty. See "Set computation controls" for every setting, including those for "laplace" and "marginal".

laplace_draws

Number of draws taken from a "laplace" or "marginal" approximation for summaries; default 2000, minimum 2. Without importance correction these are independent Gaussian or mixture draws. With it they are resampled from the weighted candidates. More draws reduce resampling noise in summaries. They do not improve the approximation or raise the importance effective sample size.

cores

Positive integer limit on parallel R worker processes. The default of 1 runs everything in the current session. Parallel fits need the optional package processx. See "Use parallel workers".

Value

An object of class multiScaleR_bayes, a list that holds the frozen model specification, the parameter layout in parameters, the call, an inference label, and inference_metadata. Fitted objects add posterior draws, diagnostics, and a record of the computation. The class page multiScaleR_bayes describes every element, shows where each parameter lives and on which scale, and explains how to back-transform it. A prepared object (method = "prepare") has no draws.

summary() returns a list described in "Read the summary output". print() shows the computation, family, number of observations, scale formulas, and stored diagnostic status, and returns x invisibly.

Choose a computation method

methodWhat it computesOptional packages
"prepare"Matches rows to landscapes and checks formulas, priors, and bins. Fits nothingNone
"sample" (default)The full posterior by NUTS, a gradient-based Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampler, run through RTMB and tmbstan with the Laplace option offRTMB, tmbstan, rstan, posterior
"slice"The same full posterior by a slice sampler written in RNone to fit. posterior (>= 1.6.0) for diagnostics
"laplace"A joint Gaussian approximation around the posterior mode, in the same unconstrained, noncentered coordinates the samplers useRTMB
"marginal"Numerical integration over one scale-group SD, with conditional Laplace approximations for every other parameterRTMB, plus posterior with importance correction

check_bayes_setup() reports whether these packages are installed. Joint Laplace and uncorrected marginal Laplace are exploratory. In matched simulations they disagreed with full sampling about annual-scale probabilities even when their own numerical checks passed. Confirm every quantity you report with "sample" or "slice". vignette("v15-bayesian-computation", package = "multiScaleR") compares the methods on one model and shows what to do when a fit struggles.

Preparation, NUTS, slice sampling, and joint Laplace accept several landscape predictors and additive or crossed random intercepts. Marginal Laplace, with or without importance correction, needs exactly one scale-group SD across all landscape predictors. A second random scale term adds another SD even when it uses the same grouping variable. The function checks this before the numerical fit begins and never switches methods for you. A model that the syntax accepts can still fail to converge, leave a scale weakly identified, or give intervals of unknown calibration.

Choose a response family

  • "nbinom2": counts with a log link. The variance is \(\mu + \mu^2/\theta\), where theta is the size (dispersion) parameter reported by summary().

  • "poisson": counts with a log link.

  • "binomial": a logit link. Supply 0 and 1 values, FALSE and TRUE, a two-level factor whose second level is a success, or cbind(successes, failures) for grouped trials. Response-scale predictions are success probabilities.

  • "gaussian": a continuous response with an identity link and an estimated residual SD.

Write the response formula

The response formula accepts the following terms.

  • Fixed covariates, factors, and offsets.

  • Additive random intercepts such as (1 | site). Each grouping variable can appear once in a formula and needs at least two levels. Use one for repeated observations at a site.

  • Products, crossings, nesting, and factor interactions with a landscape predictor, such as habitat * year or habitat:forest. habitat * year estimates a separate habitat association in each year. It changes the response coefficients only and adds no year effect to the scale formula. An interaction between two landscape predictors still has one scale model per predictor. Every expanded coefficient keeps the normal prior on R's native factor and contrast coding.

  • Transformations of fixed covariates. scale(), poly(), splines::ns(), and splines::bs() keep their training definitions, including inside nested expressions such as I(scale(temp)) and in transformed offsets. Prediction reuses those constants for single rows, batches, and effect curves. Give a namespace prefix to any custom function that reuses one of these names, or compute its predictor before fitting.

  • Arithmetic on landscape predictors and literal numbers, such as I(habitat^2). The operators +, -, *, /, and ^ and the functions exp(), log(), sqrt(), sin(), cos(), and tan() are allowed. These expressions act on the standardized kernel value after smoothing, not on raster cells, and keep the fixed reference standardization and coefficient priors.

  • Cubic splines of a landscape predictor, from splines::ns() or splines::bs() with literal fixed knots. See "Use splines of a landscape predictor".

The following stop with an error: a fixed covariate inside an expression with a landscape predictor (write the interaction habitat:forest rather than I(habitat * forest)), any other function, including nondifferentiable ones, a landscape predictor in an offset, and adaptive spline recipes. An expression that is not finite is also an error. Values are never clipped. Random slopes, spatial random fields, observation weights, zero inflation, and imperfect detection are not supported. method = "prepare" checks all of this before any optional package is needed. vignette("v07-fitting-methods", package = "multiScaleR") lists the covariate types each fitting route accepts.

Use splines of a landscape predictor

Supply literal knots and two increasing Boundary.knots, with every knot distinct and strictly inside the boundaries, for example splines::ns(habitat, knots = 0, Boundary.knots = c(-3, 3)). Knots are in the units of the standardized predictor, after the fixed reference transformation. To place knots at raw kernel-weighted values, prepare the model once with the plain predictor, then subtract prepared$specification$center and divide by prepared$specification$spread for both the knots and the boundaries. Write the resulting numbers into the formula. Never learn knots from prediction data.

Basis values and their derivatives update at every candidate scale, while the knots, the coefficient basis, and the priors stay fixed. All basis columns share the scale of their source predictor, including in factor interactions. Natural-spline tails are linear on the link scale. These are unpenalized bases of fixed complexity, with no smoothing-variance uncertainty and no monotonicity constraint. Adaptive df recipes, repeated or boundary knots, and degrees other than 3 are not supported here. The error message points to the refit backend of multiScale_optim() for those.

Write the scale formulas

Each formula in scales models the natural log of one predictor's scale. Scale formulas use columns of data. They cannot use landscape predictors, offsets, or a rank-deficient design.

  • ~1 (the default): one shared scale for all observations.

  • ~ elevation: the log scale changes linearly with a numeric covariate. exp() of its coefficient is the multiplicative change in scale per unit of the covariate.

  • ~ year: fixed effects of a factor on the log scale, coded as contrasts with the first level.

  • ~0 + year: a separate log scale for each level, each with the same distance prior, and no pooling. An intercept-free formula must define disjoint factor levels like this. Every other formula needs an intercept.

  • ~1 + (1 | year): partial pooling. Years share a typical scale and an estimated between-year SD.

Random intercepts are noncentered, so each group's deviation is a standard-normal latent value times the group SD. For ~1 + (1 | year) the scale of year \(y\) is \(\log D_y = \alpha + \tau z_y\), with \(z_y \sim N(0, 1)\). Here alpha is the log of the typical scale and tau is the SD of log scale among years. exp(tau) is a multiplier. A year one SD above typical has a scale exp(tau) times the typical one. Years are exchangeable, and the model imposes no trend or temporal autocorrelation.

The two formulas describe different parts of the model. A year effect in the response formula changes baseline abundance or occurrence. A year effect in the scale formula changes how far the landscape effect reaches.

Expand a dot in a scale formula

A dot expands every column of data, including the response and the row-ID column. Remove the response, row keys, and unrelated columns explicitly, as in ~ . - count - site_year. Only the active terms create scale coefficients and priors. A removed column adds no coefficient and no latent group coordinate. Prediction reuses the fitted active terms and does not need the removed columns. A landscape predictor of the response formula cannot also enter a scale formula.

Set the priors

SettingDefaultWhat it controls
scale_mediansqrt(inputs$min_D * inputs$max_D)Prior median of each scale, in map units. One positive number, or a named vector with one value per landscape predictor. It is the center of the normal prior on each log-scale intercept, or on each coefficient of a ~0 + year formula
scale_intercept_sd1SD of that normal prior, on the natural log scale
scale_coef_sd0.5SD of the zero-centered normal prior on other scale coefficients (slopes and log-distance contrasts)
scale_group_sd0.5Scale of the half-normal prior on each between-group SD of log scale
beta_sd2.5SD of the zero-centered normal prior on each response coefficient, on the link scale
response_group_sd1Scale of the half-normal prior on each response random-intercept SD, on the link scale
dispersion_log_mean, dispersion_log_sd0, 1Mean and SD of the normal prior on the log of NB2 theta or of the Gaussian residual SD

The scale priors act on log distances and set no hard limit at min_D or max_D. A scale beyond max_D weights the extracted neighborhood ever more evenly. It cannot draw on cells outside the prepared buffers. posterior_scales() reports the posterior mass below min_D and above max_D. Check what the priors imply with simulate_bayes_prior() before you fit. vignette("v13-bayesian-scales", package = "multiScaleR") converts these settings into distances and multipliers.

Understand the fixed standardization

Kernel means use the finite-cell numerator and denominator stored in the bins. Missing raster cells are excluded and the remaining weights renormalized. Each landscape predictor is then centered and scaled once, across the fitting rows, at its prior median scale (scale_median). That reference transformation is held fixed for every candidate scale, group, and draw, including when a site has repeated observations or scales differ among years. It is never estimated again from prediction rows. The retained values are specification$center and specification$spread.

multiScale_optim() restandardizes at each fitted scale, so the two functions give coefficients with different meanings. Here a response coefficient is the change in the linear predictor for one reference SD of the kernel-weighted predictor at scale_median, not at the fitted scale. Its prior therefore has a fixed meaning, but its value changes when you change scale_median. Report scale_median with any coefficient, and do not compare these coefficients directly with those of multiScale_optim().

Weighted surface SQ is the square root of the kernel-weighted centered variance, divided by the sum of the weights, computed over each source's finite cells. It uses the same pooled reference transformation.

Plan memory for weighted SQ

Preparation records specification$surface$memory, which gives the number of observation-cell evaluations (observation_cells), the retained buffer bytes (retained_bytes), and a planning estimate of differentiation memory (estimated_AD_bytes). Repeated observations count separately. Before a differentiation tape is recorded for SQ, a conservative check against installed RAM must pass, and the fit stops otherwise. The estimate is a planning figure, not a quota or a guarantee, so leave headroom. Candidate batches are evaluated in bounded pieces. Other optimized surface metrics are not supported.

Read the summary output

summary() of a prepared object returns inference, family, observations, and scale_formulas. For a fit with draws it returns a list with these elements.

  • inference, family, observations: the computation label, the response family, and the number of observations.

  • coefficients: a data frame with one row per response coefficient and columns mean, median, sd, lower, and upper (a central 95% credible interval). Values are on the link scale, the log expected count for Poisson and NB2, the log odds for binomial, and response units for Gaussian models. For a count model, exp() of a landscape coefficient is the multiplicative change in the expected count per reference SD of the predictor.

  • scales: the posterior_scales() table, with each scale in map units.

  • scale_coefficients: a list with one data frame per landscape predictor. Intercepts and ~0 + year coefficients are in log map units, so exp() gives a distance. Other coefficients are log-distance contrasts, so exp() gives a ratio of distances.

  • group_sd: a list with log_scale_group_sd, the between-group SD of log scale (tau) for each scale random term labeled predictor:group in term, and response_group_sd, the random-intercept SDs on the link scale. Each is NULL when the model has no such term. These SDs measure variation among groups. They are not the standard error of any one group's scale.

  • dispersion: NB2 theta or the Gaussian residual SD on its natural scale, or NULL for Poisson and binomial models.

  • diagnostics: the fit's stored checks, described on the class page multiScaleR_bayes.

Summary intervals are marginal central 95% intervals for individual quantities, not a joint band. mean and sd are summaries of the draws. For long-tailed distances, prefer median, lower, and upper. For an importance-corrected fit, the scales table uses the resampled draws. posterior_scales(fit, estimator = "weighted") summarizes the weighted candidates directly, as plot() does by default.

The stored check covers the raw parameters and, for NUTS, sampler behavior. It does not replace diagnose_bayes_scales() for the scales you report, or a posterior predictive check with simulate.multiScaleR_bayes().

Interpret weakly informed scales

A few years or regions say little about variation among them, so the group-SD prior can drive the answer. Compare plausible scale and group-SD priors, inspect posterior predictive behavior, and check the sampling diagnostics. A response coefficient near zero leaves its landscape scale weakly identified even when the chains mix well. The half-normal prior on a group SD has no point mass at zero, so a positive lower interval limit is not a test of equal scales. Compare a shared-scale model instead. Numerical accuracy depends on the response, the scale design, and the method. Interval calibration for general ecological data sets has not been established.

Use parallel workers

cores sets how many local R processes run at once. NUTS and slice sampling spread chains across workers, so the useful limit is chains. Joint and uncorrected marginal Laplace spread optimizer starts, so the limit is the number of starts. Marginal integration still visits grid nodes in order, so each node can start from the previous fits. With importance correction, workers also evaluate batches of candidate posterior densities, while proposal generation and diagnostics stay in the main process. Preparation uses one process.

Each worker holds its own copy of the model data and, where needed, its own differentiation tape, so memory use rises with cores. Temporary worker files are removed after fitting. Worker start-up and data transfer can make small fits slower. The effective limit is recorded in sampling$cores, laplace$cores, or marginal$cores.

Set computation controls

SettingMethodDefaultWhat it does
adapt_delta"sample"0.9Target acceptance rate during NUTS adaptation, strictly between 0 and 1. Raise it when transitions diverge
max_treedepth"sample"12Maximum NUTS tree depth. Raise it when the sampler hits the limit
starts"laplace", "marginal"6 for Laplace, 3 per grid node for marginalDeterministic, dispersed optimizer starts. Every start adds run time
iter.max"laplace", "marginal"1000Optimizer iterations per start
max_grid"marginal"129Largest integration grid, 33, 65, 129, or 257 nodes. More nodes cost more time
cdf_tol, quantile_tol, logz_tol"marginal"0.005, 0.02, 0.01Largest change allowed between successive grids in the SD CDF, its 2.5%, 50%, and 97.5% quantiles (in prior SDs), and the log normalizing constant
correction"marginal""none""importance" reweights the approximation against the full posterior
importance_minimportance16384Minimum number of production candidates retained
importance_maximportance65536Cap on production candidates, 16384, 32768, 65536, or 131072
importance_dfimportance7Degrees of freedom of the Student t proposal, 7 or 5
importance_refinementsimportance1Further proposal adaptations allowed after a failed stage, 0, 1, or 2
nested_responseimportanceTRUE, or FALSE with conditional_beta = TRUEIntegrate response random effects when locating conditional modes
conditional_betaimportanceFALSEExperimental. Propose response coefficients conditional on each candidate's scales and response random effects

Grid refinement stops when all three changes fall within their tolerances. It measures numerical integration error, not Laplace error.

importance_max is a cap, not a target. A population that passes its checks at a smaller size stops there. To require more candidates, as you may for precise annual quantiles, also raise importance_min, which takes the same values and cannot exceed importance_max. A separate training pilot of 16384 candidates always runs first and is discarded. Larger populations cost more, and they guarantee neither a chosen Monte Carlo error nor recovery of a missed posterior region. importance_df = 5 gives heavier proposal tails, which can help when importance ratios are unstable, though it can need more candidates. With importance_refinements = 1, a failed first production stage of 16384 candidates trains one further proposal. Its candidates are discarded and a fresh final stage is drawn. These settings change sampling efficiency, not the priors or the diagnostic thresholds.

nested_response = FALSE keeps the original joint conditional proposal, which can miss response-SD uncertainty. An explicit nested_response = TRUE requires importance correction. conditional_beta = TRUE also requires importance correction and selects nested_response = FALSE unless you supply it, so an explicit nested_response = TRUE is then an error. Gaussian coefficient conditionals are exact. Other families use a normalized Student t proposal with 7 degrees of freedom, and a fixed 20% latent-prior component guards regions the local geometry misses. Conditional optimization costs more per candidate and does not guarantee precise interval endpoints. vignette("v15-bayesian-computation", package = "multiScaleR") reports the simulation evidence for the corrected proposals and its limits.

How each computation works

Slice sampling

Slice sampling updates blocks of parameters in turn from the full posterior. For Gaussian responses it draws the regression coefficients from their exact conditional distribution. It reuses kernel values when it updates response parameters and recomputes only the changed kernel during scale updates. Efficiency depends on the data set and on dependence among scales and response effects, so compare Rhat and effective sample size per second before choosing a sampler for a larger fit.

Joint Laplace approximation

The Laplace method inverts the positive-definite Hessian of the full negative log posterior at a numerically stationary mode, including the Jacobians of the log-SD coordinates. It approximates all parameters jointly. It neither fixes the estimated pooling SDs nor integrates random effects with a nested approximation. Non-positive curvature, or failure to find a stationary mode, stops the fit with an error whose starts element keeps every attempted solution. Catch it with tryCatch() to inspect them. Distinct modes within two log-posterior units trigger a warning. Skewness, weak scale identification, and dependence between group SDs and year effects can make the pooling and the intervals inaccurate even when the checks pass. Compare important results with method = "sample", especially with few years or weak landscape effects. chains, iter, and warmup are unused.

Marginal Laplace approximation

The marginal method needs exactly one scale-group SD, such as the between-year SD in list(habitat = ~1 + (1 | year)). It integrates that SD numerically on a grid in the coordinates of its half-normal prior CDF, which leaves the prior unchanged and allows a skewed SD distribution. Every other parameter, including any response random-intercept SD, gets a conditional joint Gaussian approximation at each grid node, and the conditional posterior volume corrects the SD marginal. This is not full INLA. Linear interpolation between nodes and triangular mixture sampling give continuous SD draws and carry conditional dependence into the other parameters. The grid endpoints use SDs of 1e-8 and 8 times the prior scale. These approximate the prior CDF endpoints and do not bound the sampled SDs. The checks also fail when more than 0.001 of the posterior mass lies above prior CDF 0.9999, or more than 0.01 of the node weight carries competing conditional modes. A failed node stops the fit rather than being dropped. Conditional skewness, remaining multimodality, and response-SD uncertainty still call for comparison with full sampling.

Importance correction

control = list(correction = "importance") targets the same full posterior as NUTS by reweighting candidates from a proposal built on the marginal approximation. It does not rescale intervals by an empirical coverage factor. A training pilot draws from an equal mixture of multivariate and coordinatewise Student t distributions (7 degrees of freedom, or 5 with importance_df = 5, inflated by a factor of 1.2) and fits local proposal means and covariances. The pilot is then discarded. Production candidates come 80% from the learned proposal and 20% from the original one. Training weights are tempered and learned covariances are shrunk toward the original, which stabilizes learning without changing the target. Production weights are neither smoothed nor truncated, and every mixture density, including the prior-CDF Jacobian, enters the importance ratio. A 1% uniform component in prior-CDF coordinates keeps the proposal positive in very small tails. A further 1% normal component for the log SD, with mean log(2 * prior SD) and SD 0.6, covers SDs beyond the numerical CDF endpoints. A refinement after a failed stage fits a new component with 60% of the proposal weight and keeps 40% for the previous mixture. Training stages never enter the final estimate, though history and production_candidates keep their diagnostics and cost.

With nested response integration, outer curvature comes from central differences of RTMB's analytic gradient. With exactly one response random-intercept term, each candidate draws its site effects from independent Student t proposals with 20 degrees of freedom, centered on their conditional modes and scaled by their curvatures. This follows the dependence of site effects on the sampled response SD. Only the smaller outer covariance is stored at each SD node, which avoids dense site-by-site matrices. More response terms use an expanded joint proposal, and its reliability has not been established. Nonfinite site geometry falls back to the normalized prior proposal for that candidate and is counted. Candidates are never dropped. Unusable learned covariances keep their original nodes. The full-posterior ratios still correct these proposals, and the same checks apply.

The corrected checks require Pareto k at most 0.7, raw weight effective sample size (ESS) at least 1000, tail-indicator ESS at least 400, maximum weight at most 0.01, and split-half CDF differences at most 0.05. Indicators are evaluated at the 2.5%, 50%, and 97.5% quantiles of the unconstrained parameters, annual log scales, and group SDs. These are importance diagnostics, not MCMC Rhat or ESS. The original proposal flag stays in diagnostics$proposal_passed, but only the corrected checks decide eligibility. A finite candidate set can still miss modes or tails. A warning or a failed check calls for NUTS, and passing does not establish interval calibration.

Examples

# Annual survey example: 100 counts at 25 sites over five years, with one
# habitat map per year prepared by kernel_prep_by_group()
example <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "bayesian-annual-example.rds",
  package = "multiScaleR"))

# Check the model before fitting. Preparation matches each row to its
# landscape through row_id and needs no optional packages.
prepared <- multiScale_bayes(count ~ habitat + factor(year) + (1 | site),
  example$inputs, example$data, scales = list(habitat = ~1 + (1 | year)),
  row_id = "site_year", family = "nbinom2",
  priors = list(scale_median = 250), method = "prepare")
prepared                        # family, observations, and scale formula
#> Experimental Bayesian landscape-scale model
#> Inference: prepared 
#> Family: nbinom2 | observations: 100 
#> Scale formulas:
#>   habitat : ~1 + (1 | year) 
prepared$inference_metadata$uncertainty$intervals  # "not_provided" yet
#> [1] "not_provided"

# The same model fitted with NUTS, stored as 2,000 thinned draws
fit <- example$fits$pooled
fit_summary <- summary(fit)
fit_summary$diagnostics$passed    # TRUE: the sampler checks passed
#> [1] TRUE
# Response coefficients on the log expected-count scale
fit_summary$coefficients[c("coefficient", "median", "lower", "upper")]
#>        coefficient    median       lower     upper
#> 1      (Intercept) 2.5875680  2.34823418 2.8156719
#> 2 factor(year)2022 0.3441289  0.09189045 0.5941000
#> 3 factor(year)2023 0.1302952 -0.21349941 0.4921239
#> 4 factor(year)2024 0.1284989 -0.12032150 0.3825631
#> 5 factor(year)2025 0.4055208  0.11122988 0.6711479
#> 6          habitat 0.9068686  0.74879486 1.2338224
# Sigma for each year, in meters, after partial pooling
fit_summary$scales[c("group", "median", "lower", "upper")]
#>       group   median    lower    upper
#> 1 year=2021 173.0828 39.08530 431.8495
#> 2 year=2022 173.7422 41.71146 423.5986
#> 3 year=2023 143.6104 34.01918 376.3533
#> 4 year=2024 175.0161 41.81391 441.1051
#> 5 year=2025 155.9366 49.68400 373.9298
# Tau, the SD of log sigma among years, and the multiplier exp(tau)
fit_summary$group_sd$log_scale_group_sd[c("term", "median", "lower", "upper")]
#>           term    median      lower     upper
#> 1 habitat:year 0.2351976 0.01032759 0.8547712
exp(fit_summary$group_sd$log_scale_group_sd$median)
#> [1] 1.265159

# A slice-sampled fit with one shared sigma per layer. Its call shows the
# sampling arguments, and its scale intercepts are in log meters.
shared <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "cache-bayesian-scales.rds",
  package = "multiScaleR"))$fit
shared$call
#> multiScale_bayes(formula = counts ~ site + land1 + land2, inputs = inputs, 
#>     data = landscape_counts, family = "poisson", priors = list(scale_median = c(land1 = 300, 
#>         land2 = 300)), method = "slice", seed = 5211)
shared_coef <- summary(shared)$scale_coefficients
exp(sapply(shared_coef, function(x) x$median))   # median sigma in meters
#>    land1    land2 
#> 246.6455 501.1973 
# See vignette("v13-bayesian-scales", package = "multiScaleR") for fitting
# and interpretation.
